---
title: "Set up your coding buddy"
---

Last year you asked an AI tutor questions and typed every line of code
yourself. This year you also get a **coding agent**, a program that reads your
project, changes your files, and runs commands in your terminal. This chapter
puts one on your machine and connects it to the model your school provides. You
do this once, at the start of the year.

The course suggests `pi`, an open source agent you run in a terminal, from
[pi.dev](https://pi.dev). It is deliberately minimal. Out of the box it edits
files and runs shell commands, and almost everything past that you add
yourself. Behind `pi` sits the model that does the actual thinking, Qwen 3.8
27B, served by your school's Novedu platform.

## What a small model means for you {#sec-buddy-setup-model}

By the standards of 2026, Qwen 3.8 27B is a small model. It writes decent
TypeScript and it follows clear instructions, and it gets lost when a task runs
long or a prompt stays vague. Cutting a job into steps the model can finish in
one turn is the skill you are here for, and a bigger model would let you skip
that practice by absorbing your sloppy prompt anyway. Nobody is billing you for
a run that goes wrong either, so a bad answer costs you one retry.

## Install pi {#sec-buddy-setup-install}

The installation is your first research task of the year. Open
[pi.dev](https://pi.dev), find the install instructions for your operating
system, and follow them. Install commands change faster than a book can be
reprinted, which is why this page does not copy them. Then open a fresh
terminal and check that `pi` starts. If the terminal does not know the
command, the documentation on pi.dev has a section for that too, and so does
any search engine.

## Tell pi where the model is {#sec-buddy-setup-models}

`pi` keeps its settings in a folder named `.pi/agent` inside your home folder.
Two files in that folder matter. The first, `models.json`, says where the Novedu
endpoint is and what the model is called. It is the same for everybody in the
course, so copy it as it is:

```json
{{< include ../models.json >}}
```

Save it as `~/.pi/agent/models.json`. On Windows that path reads
`C:\Users\<you>\.pi\agent\models.json`. Create the folder if it is missing.

## Add your key {#sec-buddy-setup-key}

The second file, `auth.json`, holds your key. You pick that key up yourself,
from the buddy for Part 2, the DOM, which is the part that starts right after
this chapter.

{{< coding coding-buddy-dom >}}

The page also shows a server address and a model name. You already have both,
in the `models.json` you just saved, so the key is the only thing you still
need from it. Create `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` with this content and paste your
key in place of the placeholder:

```json
{
  "novedu": {
    "type": "api_key",
    "key": "nvk-your-own-key-goes-here"
  }
}
```

Keys start with `nvk-`, so a value that looks different is the wrong string.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The key is yours

Treat the key like a password. Do not post it anywhere, and do not commit
`auth.json` into a git repository. Nobody else in the class has your key, so a
key that turns up somewhere else came from you. If `pi` reports an
authentication error and the key matches what the page gave you, your teacher
has closed the activity. Fetching the key again gives you the same one, so
that is a question for your teacher, not for the page.
:::

## A new key for every part {#sec-buddy-setup-new-part}

Each part of the book has its own coding buddy, and each buddy hands out its
own key. The chapter that opens a part carries the link, so you pick the next
key up the same way you picked up this one. Open `~/.pi/agent/auth.json`, paste
the new key in place of the old one, and start `pi` again, because it reads the
file at startup. `models.json` never changes.

## Start pi for the first time {#sec-buddy-setup-first-start}

`pi` works in the folder you start it from, so open a terminal in a folder you
do not mind the agent reading. Your `hello-page` project from the previous
chapter is a good one. Start the agent:

```bash
pi
```

Pick the model with `/model` and choose *Coding buddy for the Creative Coding 2
course*. Then type any message at all and press Enter. You are checking one
thing here: whether a reply comes back.

::: {.callout-warning}
## When pi just sits there

The model runs on an endpoint your whole school shares, and a request sometimes
never comes back. There is no error and no retry, the session simply hangs
before printing anything, and the same failure also shows up as an empty answer
after a minute or two. Wait a couple of minutes, press `Escape`, and send the
same message again. It is not your prompt and it is not your machine.
:::

Five commands and keys carry you through the year.

* `/model` picks the model for the session.
* `/new` throws away the conversation so far and starts an empty one.
* `!<command>` runs a shell command without leaving `pi`, so you can check
  `ls` or `git status` yourself instead of asking the agent what is in the
  folder.
* `Escape` stops the agent in the middle of a turn.
* `Ctrl+D` closes `pi` when the input line is empty.

`/help` lists the other slash commands, and the documentation on
[pi.dev](https://pi.dev) explains what `/help` only names.

## Other agents work too {#sec-buddy-setup-other-agents}

`pi` is a suggestion, not a rule. Any coding agent that can talk to an
OpenAI-compatible endpoint reaches the course model, for example
[little-coder](https://github.com/itayinbarr/little-coder) or
[opencode](https://opencode.ai). Whatever you pick needs the same four
settings:

* the base URL `https://novedu.at/api/coding/v1`
* an OpenAI chat completions API, which most agents call "OpenAI compatible"
* the model id `coding`
* your key from the connection page as the API key

Finding where your agent wants those four is your own job, and that hunt
through someone's documentation is exactly the research this course asks of you
all year. Two things come with the choice. Every chapter of this book that
shows a command shows a `pi` command, and your teacher does not debug other
agents during class.

## Where you stand {#sec-buddy-setup-done}

`pi` runs on your machine, it knows where the model lives, and it answers when
you type. Part 2 starts on the next page and takes the page apart element by
element. The chapter on actually working with the buddy comes later in that
part, once you have code worth handing to it.
